q: What is the IUPAC name of the ether shown?
h: Name an ether as an alkoxy substituent on the larger alkyl group, then find the longest chain of that group.
w: The larger alkyl group (four carbons) is the parent alkane and the smaller group becomes the alkoxy substituent: CH3CH2O– is ethoxy. The four-carbon chain is numbered so the ethoxy carbon gets the lowest number, C2. The name is 2-ethoxybutane (common name: sec-butyl ethyl ether).
x: 1-Ethoxybutane has the oxygen on the end carbon of an unbranched butyl group; here the O is on C2 of the four-carbon chain.
The parent should be the larger alkyl group (butane), with the smaller ethyl group named as ethoxy.
Calling the chain "propane" with a methyl branch misses the longest chain; the C1 methyl plus three more carbons make a butane chain.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Count the ring atoms (including O) and remember that the ring oxygen is position 1.
w: A three-membered ring with one oxygen is an oxirane (epoxide). Numbering starts at the oxygen (O1), so the substituted carbon is C2: 2-methyloxirane (also called propylene oxide or 1,2-epoxypropane).
x: Oxetane is the four-membered cyclic ether; this ring has only two carbons and one oxygen.
The ring oxygen is O1 and numbering goes the short way to the substituent, so the methyl carbon is C2, not C3.
The molecule has three carbons in all, so as an epoxy-alkane it is 1,2-epoxypropane, not epoxybutane.

q: Which pair of reagents gives the best yield of the ether shown by a Williamson synthesis?
h: The Williamson synthesis is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. Which carbon can be attacked from the back side?
w: A Williamson ether synthesis is SN2: the alkoxide attacks an alkyl halide with a good leaving group. Put the hindered group on the alkoxide and the unhindered group on the halide. tert-Butoxide + bromoethane works because the primary C–Br carbon is open to back-side attack.
x: A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; ethoxide acts as a base and the main product is 2-methylpropene by E2.
An alcohol has no leaving group (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group), so ethoxide only does an acid–base exchange with it.
Ethanol has no leaving group, so tert-butoxide simply deprotonates it (an acid–base equilibrium), not a substitution.

q: What is the major organic product of this reaction?
h: Can a strong base reach the back side of a tertiary carbon? If not, what else can it do?
w: Ethoxide is a strong base and a good nucleophile, but a tertiary carbon is too hindered for SN2. With a strong base and a 3° halide, E2 wins: ethoxide removes a β-H and bromide leaves, giving 2-methylpropene. This is why a Williamson synthesis must use a methyl or primary halide.
x: This ether would need S<sub>N</sub>2 at a tertiary carbon, which is blocked; it is made instead from tert-butoxide and a primary ethyl halide.
There is no water or hydroxide as a nucleophile, and the strong base favors E2 over the slow S<sub>N</sub>1 path.
Forming this ether would need tert-butoxide and a tertiary electrophile; neither is present, and such a hindered ether is not made by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Which reagents give the best preparation of the aryl ether shown?
h: One of the two carbons on oxygen is sp<sup>2</sup>. Can that carbon be the S<sub>N</sub>2 electrophile?
w: The Williamson synthesis needs back-side attack on an sp3 carbon. The aryl carbon cannot be the electrophile, so the aryl group must be on the nucleophile: phenoxide (easily made because phenol has pKa ≈ 10) attacks iodoethane by SN2. Sodium phenoxide + iodoethane is the best choice.
x: Aryl halides do not do S<sub>N</sub>2: the ring blocks back-side attack and the C(sp<sup>2</sup>)–Br bond is strong. No ether forms with an unactivated bromobenzene.
Ethoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) just deprotonates phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10) to give phenoxide and ethanol; no C–O bond forms.
Ethanol has no leaving group, so phenoxide cannot displace anything from it.

q: What is the main product when this bromo alcohol is treated with NaH in THF?
h: NaH makes the alkoxide. Count the atoms that will end up in the ring, including O.
w: NaH deprotonates the OH. The alkoxide then attacks the primary C–Br carbon in the same molecule (intramolecular Williamson, SN2). The new ring holds O plus C1–C5: a six-membered ring, oxane (tetrahydropyran). Five- and six-membered rings form quickly because the chain ends meet easily and there is little ring strain.
x: Oxolane has only four carbons; the ring here includes all five chain carbons plus the oxygen.
Oxepane is a seven-membered ring (six carbons); the chain has only five carbons.
E2 on a primary bromide with an alkoxide is minor; the fast intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 that forms a six-membered ring wins.

q: (S)-4-Bromopentan-1-ol is treated with NaH in THF. What is the main product?
h: The ring closes by S<sub>N</sub>2 at the carbon bearing Br. What does S<sub>N</sub>2 do to that stereocenter?
w: NaH forms the alkoxide, which attacks C4 from the back side (intramolecular SN2), making a five-membered ring (O + 4 C). Back-side attack inverts C4. The oxygen takes the place of Br as the top-priority group, so the descriptor changes from S to (R)-2-methyloxolane (confirmed with CIP ranking: O > ring CH2 > CH3 > H).
x: Retention would need front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 ring closure inverts the carbon that loses bromide.
Racemization needs a carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1). A secondary bromide with a strong internal nucleophile reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 with clean inversion.
E2 can compete at a secondary bromide, but 5-membered ring closure is intramolecular and fast, so the cyclic ether is the main product.

q: What is the major product of this alkoxymercuration–demercuration?
h: Methanol adds to the alkene carbon that can best carry positive charge in the mercurinium ion.
w: Alkoxymercuration adds RO and H across C=C with Markovnikov regiochemistry and no rearrangement. Methanol opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon (the one with more partial positive charge), and NaBH4 replaces Hg with H. The product is 1-methoxy-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the anti-Markovnikov ether; methanol adds to the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, not the secondary one.
The solvent is methanol, not water, so the nucleophile that adds is CH<sub>3</sub>OH and an ether forms, not an alcohol.
Mercurinium ions do not rearrange, so the methoxy group cannot move to C3.

q: What is the major product?
h: Does a bridged mercurinium ion allow a methyl shift the way a free carbocation would?
w: Ethanol opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon (C2), and NaBH4 replaces Hg by H. Because the mercurinium ion is bridged, there is no free carbocation and no methyl shift. The product is 2-ethoxy-3,3-dimethylbutane. (Acid-catalyzed addition of ethanol would instead give the rearranged 2-ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane.)
x: This rearranged ether forms only through a free 2° carbocation and a 1,2-methyl shift, which the bridged mercurinium ion avoids.
This is anti-Markovnikov addition; the alcohol attacks the more substituted carbon of the mercurinium ion.
An alcohol would form with water as solvent (oxymercuration); in ethanol the nucleophile is ethanol, giving an ether.

q: Methoxybenzene (anisole) is heated with excess HI. What are the products?
h: After protonation, iodide must do an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack. Which carbon on oxygen can it attack?
w: HI protonates the ether oxygen. Iodide then attacks by SN2, and it can only attack the sp3 methyl carbon; aryl carbons do not undergo SN2 or SN1. So the aryl C–O bond stays and the products are phenol + iodomethane. Phenol is not converted further, because its C–O bond cannot be broken this way.
x: Cleaving the aryl C–O bond would need S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1 at an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon, which does not happen.
Phenol cannot be converted to iodobenzene by HI; only the alkyl side of the ether is cleaved.
With excess HI the methyl group leaves as iodomethane (I<sup>−</sup> attacks the methyl carbon directly), not as methanol.

q: Tetrahydrofuran (oxolane) is heated with excess concentrated HBr. What is the final organic product?
h: The first cleavage opens the ring. What happens to the new OH group with more HBr?
w: Protonation of O and SN2 attack by Br− at a primary carbon opens the ring to 4-bromobutan-1-ol. With excess HBr and heat, that primary alcohol is protonated and displaced by a second bromide. The final product is 1,4-dibromobutane.
x: 4-Bromobutan-1-ol is the intermediate after one equivalent; excess HBr converts its OH to Br as well.
HBr does not reduce C–O to C–H; one carbon end would have to lose its oxygen without gaining bromine.
Water is not the nucleophile here; bromide attacks the protonated ether, and diols are converted to dibromides by excess HBr.

q: tert-Butyl methyl ether is treated with one equivalent of HI. Which products form?
h: After protonation, one C–O bond can break without any nucleophile. Which one gives the more stable cation?
w: Protonation makes a good leaving group. The tertiary C–O bond ionizes (SN1) to the stable tert-butyl cation and methanol leaves; iodide then traps the cation. Products: 2-iodo-2-methylpropane + methanol. The methyl C–O bond would need an SN2 attack, which is slower than ionization here.
x: This would be S<sub>N</sub>2 at the methyl group. For ethers with a tertiary group, S<sub>N</sub>1 cleavage at the 3° carbon is faster.
Converting both groups to iodides needs a second equivalent of HI; with one equivalent the methanol remains.
The methyl group leaves as methanol, not iodomethane; and E1 (2-methylpropene) would pair with methanol, not iodomethane.

q: The diether shown is heated with excess HBr. Which set of products forms?
h: Treat each C–O bond separately: which ones have an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon that bromide can attack?
w: Each protonated ether is cleaved by SN2 attack of Br− on an sp3 carbon. The Ar–O bond cannot break, so the aryl side gives phenol. The CH3–O and both CH2–O bonds can be attacked; with excess HBr every alkyl alcohol formed is also converted to its bromide, giving 1,3-dibromopropane and bromomethane.
x: Bromobenzene cannot form: the aryl C–O bond is not cleaved because aryl carbons do not do S<sub>N</sub>1 or S<sub>N</sub>2.
HBr cleavage makes alkyl bromides, not alcohols, once excess acid and heat convert the alkyl OH groups.
The aryl C–O bond stays intact, and with excess HBr the 3-bromopropanol OH is also replaced by Br.

q: The crown ether shown (18-crown-6) binds which cation most strongly?
h: Match the size of the cavity to the size of the ion.
w: Crown ethers bind cations whose diameter fits the ring cavity, with all oxygen lone pairs pointing inward. The 18-membered ring with six oxygens fits K+ best. (15-crown-5 fits Na+, 12-crown-4 fits Li+.)
x: Li<sup>+</sup> is too small for the 18-crown-6 cavity; 12-crown-4 is the better size match.
Na<sup>+</sup> is somewhat small for 18-crown-6; 15-crown-5 fits it better.
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is small and very strongly hydrated, and it does not fit the 18-crown-6 cavity well.

q: KF barely reacts with 1-bromooctane in acetonitrile, but adding a little 18-crown-6 gives 1-fluorooctane quickly. What is the best explanation?
c: The crown ether binds K<sup>+</sup>, bringing KF into solution with a poorly solvated, very reactive F<sup>−</sup>
The crown ether binds F<sup>−</sup> through its oxygens and delivers it directly to the carbon
The crown ether hydrogen-bonds to F<sup>−</sup>, making it a stronger base and nucleophile
The crown ether coordinates the Br, making bromide a better leaving group
h: The oxygen lone pairs of a crown ether point into its cavity. Which ion do they attract?
w: The ring oxygens are Lewis bases that wrap around K+. The large organic-coated complex dissolves in the organic solvent and drags F− with it. That fluoride has no tight cation partner and no hydrogen-bonding shell ("naked" fluoride), so it is a much stronger nucleophile and SN2 is fast. The crown ether binds K+.
x: Oxygen lone pairs attract cations, not anions; the crown ether does not bind fluoride.
A crown ether has no O–H groups, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to fluoride; hydrogen bonding would also make F<sup>−</sup> less reactive.
The crown ether does not interact with the alkyl bromide; its role is to bind the potassium ion.

q: (Z)-Hex-3-ene is treated with mCPBA. Which describes the product?
h: Epoxidation is concerted: both C–O bonds form on the same face at the same time.
w: Peroxyacid epoxidation is a concerted syn addition, so the alkene geometry is kept: a Z alkene gives a cis-epoxide. cis-2,3-Diethyloxirane has two stereocenters (R,S) and a mirror plane, so it is a single meso compound; attack on either face gives the same molecule.
x: trans-Epoxides come from E alkenes; the concerted reaction cannot rotate the C–C bond.
A mixture of cis and trans would need a stepwise path with a rotating intermediate; mCPBA epoxidation is stereospecific.
The cis-epoxide here has identical groups on both carbons and a mirror plane, so it is meso; there is no enantiomer pair.

q: (E)-But-2-ene is treated with Br2 in water, and the product is then treated with NaOH. What is the final product?
h: Follow the stereochemistry of two anti steps: anti halohydrin formation, then back-side ring closure.
w: Step 1 adds Br and OH anti (bromonium ion opened by water), giving the bromohydrin. In step 2 the alkoxide attacks the C–Br carbon from the back side (intramolecular SN2), which needs O− and Br anti. Anti addition followed by an anti (back-side) ring closure puts the oxygen on the same face overall, exactly as mCPBA would. The E alkene therefore gives racemic trans-2,3-dimethyloxirane.
x: A cis-epoxide comes from (Z)-but-2-ene; this two-step route keeps the alkene geometry just like mCPBA.
Hydroxide closes the halohydrin to an epoxide; opening it to the diol would need acid or much harsher conditions.
NaOH deprotonates the bromohydrin OH, and the alkoxide quickly displaces the anti bromide to close the epoxide.

q: What is the major product when 2,2-dimethyloxirane reacts with methanol containing a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: In the protonated epoxide, which C–O bond is longer and carries more positive charge?
w: Acid protonates the epoxide oxygen. The C–O bond to the tertiary carbon is weakened most, and that carbon carries most of the positive charge (SN1-like transition state), so methanol attacks the more substituted carbon. Product: 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.
x: This is the base-catalyzed regiochemistry (attack at the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>), which applies with CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>, not with acid.
Methanol, not water, is the solvent and nucleophile, so a methyl ether forms rather than the diol.
Only one equivalent of methanol adds; the new primary alcohol is not converted to a methyl ether under these mild conditions.

q: 2,2-Dimethyloxirane is treated with sodium ethanethiolate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SNa) in ethanol, followed by water. What is the major product?
h: A strong, unprotonated nucleophile opens an epoxide by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon is easier to reach?
w: Thiolate is a strong nucleophile, so the epoxide opens by SN2 without acid. SN2 attack occurs at the less hindered CH2 carbon, and the alkoxide is then protonated. Product: 1-(ethylsulfanyl)-2-methylpropan-2-ol.
x: Attack at the tertiary carbon is the acid-catalyzed regiochemistry; under basic S<sub>N</sub>2 conditions the hindered carbon is avoided.
Water is added only to protonate the alkoxide after the ring has opened; the thiolate is the nucleophile.
Ethanol is a much weaker nucleophile than ethanethiolate, which is large, polarizable and anionic.

q: The racemic epoxide shown (one enantiomer drawn) is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which structure is the major product (formed as a racemate; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: Decide two things: which carbon methanol attacks under acid, and from which face relative to the epoxide oxygen.
w: Under acid the nucleophile attacks the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, which carries more positive charge in the protonated epoxide. The attack is still back-side, so OCH3 ends up trans to the OH (anti opening; on the ring the product first forms with OCH3 and OH trans-diaxial). Product: trans-2-methoxy-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: B has OCH<sub>3</sub> and OH cis; epoxide opening is back-side (anti), so the two groups must be trans.
C has methanol attacking the secondary carbon, the regiochemistry seen with methoxide (base), not with acid.
Methanol, not water, is the nucleophile, so a methyl ether forms rather than a diol.
